titulo: The two conjugations: How to tell the conjugation

aula.objetivo: Recognise the 1st and 2nd conjugations, conjugate verbs in the present tense without mixing up the endings, and learn the most common irregular verbs.

blocos.titulo: The four types of verb in the present
blocos.explicacao: The four types of verb in the present. To make them easier to memorise, let's sort the present-tense verbs into four types. Type 1: ЗНАТЬ (the most common). Verbs in -ать and -ять (plus a few in -еть, such as уметь) that take the endings -ю, -ешь, -ет, -ем, -ете, -ют. Type 2: ГОВОРИТЬ (verbs in -ить and most verbs in -еть). They take the endings -ю, -ишь, -ит, -им, -ите, -ят. Type 1B: ЖИТЬ (verbs whose stem ends in a consonant). They take endings similar to the first conjugation, but with -у in the first person singular (instead of -ю). Attention: when the stress falls on the ending, the letter е becomes ё (живёшь, живёт, живём, живёте). That does not change the ending, only the pronunciation; it is a spelling convention. Type 2B: irregular verbs (few, but important). хоте́ть (to want): хочу́, хо́чешь, хо́чет, хоти́м, хоти́те, хотя́т. This verb is a mixture of both conjugations. есть (to eat): ем, ешь, ест, еди́м, еди́те, едя́т. пить (to drink): пью, пьёшь, пьёт, пьём, пьёте, пьют. дать (to give): дам, дашь, даст, дади́м, дади́те, даду́т. English has almost no verb endings (only -s in "he works"), so Russian looks heavy at first. The good news: there are only two main sets of endings, and you can choose between them by looking at the infinitive.

blocos.titulo: Exceptions: 11 verbs in -ать/-ять/-еть of the 2nd conjugation
blocos.explicacao: The exceptions: the 11 verbs in -ать/-ять/-еть that go to the 2nd conjugation. Here is a list few materials give. There are eleven verbs that end in -ать, -ять or -еть but do not follow the 1st conjugation. They follow the 2nd. How to memorise them? A tip: almost all of these verbs have a connotation of perception (see, hear, look, breathe) or feeling (hate, offend, endure). It is not an absolute rule, but it helps. Memorise them.

blocos.explicacao: The stress that wanders (or stays put). As with the adjective, the stress of the verb can move, or stay in the same place. Look: • 1. blocos.titulo: The verb TO BE (быть): the most famous absence in Russian
blocos.explicacao: The verb TO BE (быть): the most famous absence in Russian. This is the biggest surprise for English speakers. Pay attention. In Russian, the verb TO BE (быть) does not exist in the present tense. In English we say: I am Brazilian. He is a doctor. We are students. In Russian, the verb disappears: Я брази́лец. (I Brazilian.) Он врач. (He doctor.) Мы студе́нты. (We students.) The verb "to be" simply does not appear. The context does its job. It is as if the sentence were "I Brazilian", "He doctor". Russian does not miss it at all. But note one exception: the 3rd person singular of быть — есть — survives with a special meaning: "there is", "exists", "has". This is the form you will use in the construction for "to have" (next section).

blocos.titulo: How to say "I have", "you have", "he has"
blocos.explicacao: How to say "I have", "you have", "he has". This is one of the biggest differences between English and Russian, and one of the first things you will want to say. Pay attention. In everyday Russian there is no verb "to have" like the English one. Instead, Russian uses a construction that, translated literally, means "by me there is": У меня́ есть кни́га. = I have a book. (Literally: "By me there is a book".) Let me take the formula apart: У = a preposition meaning "by", "at the place of", "in the possession of". меня́ = "me" (a special form of the pronoun "I" used after у). есть = "there is", "exists" (the surviving form of the verb to be). кни́га = "book" (the thing possessed). The structure is always the same. See it with all the pronouns: Notice how the pronoun changes after у: Why does it change? It is a grammar matter you will understand later, when we study the cases. For now, memorise the forms as a formula. That is how it is said. Full stop. The good news: the formula is fixed. Always у + special form + есть + object. No mystery. Can the word "есть" be left out? Yes, in informal contexts or when the possession is obvious: У меня́ кни́га. (I have a book.) У тебя́ вре́мя? (Do you have time?) But in general, use есть while you are learning. Russians understand perfectly and you will not risk sounding odd. How to negate: To say "I don't have", Russian uses нет instead of есть: У меня́ нет кни́ги. (I don't have a book.) У тебя́ нет вре́мени? (Don't you have time?) У него́ нет маши́ны. (He doesn't have a car.) Careful: the word after нет changes form. That is a subject for a future lesson. For now, memorise the most common examples: The logic is: when affirmative, use есть + the normal object; when negative, use нет + a "modified" object. You will learn how to modify it later, but you can already memorise these ready-made formulas.

blocos.explicacao: Complete sentences: the first dialogues. Now that you know the subject pronouns, the two conjugations, the absence of the verb to be and the construction for "to have", you can form complete sentences. Dialogue 1 — In class: — Что ты де́лаешь? (What are you doing?) — Я чита́ю кни́гу. (I am reading a book.) — А он? (And he?) — Он пи́шет упражне́ние. (He is writing an exercise.) — А они́? (And they?) — Они́ говоря́т по-ру́сски. (They are speaking Russian.) Dialogue 2 — At home: — Где ты живёшь? (Where do you live?) — Я живу́ в Москве́. (I live in Moscow.) — А твоя́ семья́? (And your family?) — Они́ живу́т в Санкт-Петербу́рге. (They live in St Petersburg.) Dialogue 3 — At work: — Кто э́то? (Who is this?) — Э́то мой друг. Он рабо́тает здесь. (This is my friend. He works here.) — Он зна́ет ру́сский язы́к? (Does he know Russian?) — Да, немно́го. (Yes, a little.) Dialogue 4 — The verb "to have": — У тебя́ есть вре́мя? (Do you have time?) — Да, есть. А что? (Yes, I do. Why?) — У меня́ есть вопро́с. (I have a question.) — Хорошо́, спра́шивай. (All right, ask.) Dialogue 5 — Introducing yourself: — Приве́т! Как тебя́ зову́т? (Hi! What is your name?) — Меня́ зову́т Ива́н. А тебя́? (My name is Ivan. And yours?) — Меня́ зову́т Мари́я. Я изуча́ю ру́сский язы́к. (My name is Maria. I study Russian.) — Я то́же изуча́ю ру́сский. (I also study Russian.) Note: "Как тебя́ зову́т?" literally means "How do they call you?": the verb звать (to call) is in the 3rd person plural. The answer is Меня́ зову́т... ("They call me..."). It is the fixed formula for "What is your name?" in Russian. Memorise it as a block.

blocos.titulo: How to recognise the conjugation from the infinitive
blocos.explicacao: Practical rules: verbs in -ить are 2nd conjugation (говорить, любить, платить). Verbs in -еть are almost all 2nd conjugation (смотреть, видеть, сидеть), with exceptions such as «уметь» (умею) and «хотеть» (mixed). Verbs in -ать and -ять are almost all 1st conjugation (читать, делать, гулять), except a few 2nd-conjugation exceptions: слышать, держать, дышать, лежать, стоять. Verbs in -овать and -евать are 1st conjugation and change to -ую (рисовать → рисую). Verbs in -авать are 1st conjugation (вставать → встаю). In the 2nd conjugation, some consonants change ONLY in the «я» form: б → бл (любить → люблю), в → вл (готовить → готовлю), д → ж (видеть → вижу), т → ч (платить → плачу), с → ш (просить → прошу). The other forms stay regular: любишь, видишь.
